description: Hi, hope you wanna be on my team.
summary:
Two Small Steps is a free browser game for kids aged 7–12 that turns real mission constraints into decisions a crew must make together.

In Level 1, players drive Apollo 15's rover on the Moon. The rare rock costs most of their spare oxygen, and Mission Control answers in 2.6 seconds. In Level 2, two players run a Mars outpost, and each sees half the problem: Engineering the power fault, Protection a real solar storm (NASA DONKI, 20 May 2024). There is time for one job, and Earth's answer takes 40 minutes, so the crew decides alone. Power, oxygen and radiation are linked: low power means fewer oxygen tanks tomorrow and a smaller harvest later. A replayable free mission draws storms from real NASA records, and no plan always wins.

Every number is tagged as a NASA measurement, a calculation or a game rule. The game uses DONKI, Curiosity RAD, BVAD, OSDR and Apollo 15 data, plus live NASA requests during play.

It matters because kids rarely see the trade-offs behind a mission. Here they predict, decide together and live with the consequences. Nothing ever says "you lose", and nothing leaves the device.
details:
Two Small Steps is a free browser game for kids aged 7–12, played alone or by two players on one screen. It takes about 15 minutes, with no download and no account.

  • Level 1, the Moon (Apollo 15, 1971). Players drive the lunar rover to one of two rock sites. The far site has a rare white rock like Apollo 15's Genesis Rock, but bringing it back uses most of the oxygen they'd need to walk home. Mission Control answers in 2.6 seconds: on the Moon, Earth can still help.
  • Level 2, a Mars outpost. Two roles each report half of the problem: Engineering sees a power fault, Protection sees a solar storm coming. There is time for one job, reinforce the shelter or repair the power, and both players must vote for the same one. Earth's answer needs 40 minutes and the storm arrives in 30, so the crew decides alone.
  • Linked resources. Power, oxygen and radiation are connected. With a power unit off, the oxygen machine fills fewer tanks overnight and the greenhouse lamp stays off. The choice shows up the next sol and again on harvest day.
  • Free mission. A three-sol mission that is different every time, with storm cards drawn from real NASA DONKI events. It ends in "Mission goals met" or "Mission strained", with one star per goal met. Players predict the outcome before each decision and see whether they were right the next morning.
  • NASA terminal. During play, it fetches live data from NASA DONKI and the NASA Image Library. On the bonus sol, today's real space weather decides whether a storm comes.

NASA data

The game uses DONKI, Curiosity RAD, the Apollo 15 Mission Report and Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, NASA's Life Support Baseline Values (BVAD), MOXIE, Veggie, the Human Research Program risk ratings, OSDR study OSD-342, the NSSDCA fact sheets and JPL Horizons. Every number on screen is tagged as a Measurement, a Calculation or a Game rule, and a "NASA data" screen lists each source. Archived data is always labelled as archived.

Benefits and intended impact

Kids rarely see the decisions behind a mission, only its results. The game makes each trade-off concrete and costly. Players predict first, decide together and live with the consequence the next day, the opposite of the instant rewards common in screen content.

The two roles practise what NASA rates among the highest human risks for Mars: teamwork and working without Earth's help. Nobody "loses": hard missions end as "Mission strained", and the Commander offers hints that step back once the crew masters the strategy.

A one-page teacher card supports a 15-minute class session. A crew logbook, stored only on the device, tracks predictions, goals met and how often both reports were read. Our next step is a pilot in Hermosillo schools. We have not yet tested the game with children and make no claims about learning results.

Tools

  • Godot Engine 4.7 (GDScript), exported to WebAssembly and hosted on GitHub Pages
  • Python (pandas, Matplotlib) to download and analyse the NASA and context data
  • A Monte Carlo simulation of 20,000 missions to balance the game, and a built-in 300-mission self-test (274 met the goals)
  • Human-made art: Kenney and KayKit (CC0), game-icons.net (CC BY), and NASA's own 3D models of Earth, the Moon and Mars
  • Fonts: Atkinson Hyperlegible and Fredoka
  • The team used AI assistants (Claude, Gemini) to help with code, analysis and writing. No AI-generated images are used.

Creativity

  • The communication delay is the core mechanic: the Moon-to-Mars jump turns "Earth helps" into "the crew decides alone".
  • Split information means neither child can solve the problem alone.
  • Today's choice carries into tomorrow's oxygen and food.
  • Real NASA records drive the storms, including a live request about today's Sun.

Factors we considered

  • Age: plain language, with terms like sol, radiation dose and microgravity explained in context.
  • Accessibility: English and Spanish, device text-to-speech, touch controls, a less-motion setting and a font designed for low-vision readers.
  • Honesty about data: simplifications such as storm frequency and shelter strength are labelled as game rules, and nothing archived is shown as live.
  • Privacy: no accounts, no analytics, nothing leaves the browser.
  • Fair design: no choice is free and no plan always wins. The balance was verified by simulation.
